title: Three enzyme inhibitors
passage:
Researchers studied a liver enzyme that converts substrate S into product P. They measured initial reaction rates across a range of substrate concentrations, first with no inhibitor and then with each of three inhibitors (X, Y and Z) at a fixed concentration. They fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]), to find the apparent Km and Vmax (Table 1).

In a separate test, inhibitor X's effect disappeared when substrate concentration was raised very high. Inhibitor Z bound the enzyme only after the substrate was already bound.
cap: Table 1. Kinetic constants with and without inhibitors.

qs.q: Inhibitor X is most likely a:
qs.a: Competitive inhibitor
w: Noncompetitive inhibitor
Uncompetitive inhibitor
Irreversible inhibitor that destroys the enzyme
qs.e: Km rises while Vmax stays the same, and high substrate overcomes the inhibition, which is the signature of competitive inhibition at the active site.

qs.q: Inhibitor Y most likely:
qs.a: Binds equally well to the free enzyme and the enzyme–substrate complex
w: Competes with the substrate for binding at the enzyme's active site
Binds only to the enzyme–substrate complex and never to free enzyme
Increases the enzyme's apparent affinity for its substrate at all levels
qs.e: Vmax drops while Km is unchanged, which is the pattern of a (pure) noncompetitive inhibitor.

qs.q: With no inhibitor and [S] = 2.0 mM, what is the initial reaction rate?
qs.a: 50 µmol/min
w: 100 µmol/min
25 µmol/min
200 µmol/min
qs.e: When [S] = Km, v = Vmax / 2 = 50 µmol/min.

qs.q: Why does inhibitor Z lower both apparent Km and apparent Vmax?
qs.a: It binds only the ES complex, pulling binding toward ES while blocking product formation
w: It competes with the substrate at the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach Vmax
It binds only the free enzyme, which blocks substrate entry and slows the overall reaction
It denatures the enzyme permanently, removing active enzyme and changing its binding site
qs.e: Uncompetitive inhibitors remove ES from the pathway. By Le Châtelier's principle, more E + S form ES (apparent Km falls), while fewer complexes can make product (Vmax falls).

title: A recessive disorder in several families
passage:
Genetic counselors studied a rare disorder that causes thick mucus in the lungs and pancreas. Across 40 families, affected children were usually born to two unaffected parents. Males and females were affected at similar rates. The disorder showed up more often in families where the parents were cousins.

Sequencing showed that most affected children carried two copies of a mutant allele with a 3-nucleotide deletion in the coding region of a gene for a chloride channel. The deletion removes a single amino acid, and the misfolded channel protein is mostly destroyed before reaching the cell membrane.

qs.q: Which mode of inheritance best fits the family data?
qs.a: Autosomal recessive
w: Autosomal dominant
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
qs.e: Unaffected parents having affected children points to a recessive trait. Equal rates in males and females points to an autosome. Marriage between cousins raises the chance both parents carry the same rare allele.

qs.q: Two unaffected parents have one affected child. Their next child is born unaffected. What is the chance that this unaffected child is a carrier?
qs.e: Both parents must be carriers (Aa × Aa). Among unaffected children (AA, Aa, Aa), 2 out of 3 are carriers.

qs.q: Why does the 3-nucleotide deletion NOT cause a frameshift?
qs.a: Removing exactly one codon keeps the downstream reading frame in register
w: The deletion falls in an intron that is later spliced out of the mRNA
The degenerate code lets the ribosome skip over the three missing bases
Chloride channel genes are translated without a fixed reading frame
qs.e: Deleting a multiple of three bases removes whole codons, so the amino acids after the deletion are still read correctly.

qs.q: The misfolded channel is destroyed before reaching the cell membrane. Which cellular system is most likely responsible?
qs.a: Quality control in the ER, followed by degradation in the proteasome
w: Lysosomal enzymes after the channel is inserted into the plasma membrane
Peroxisomal enzymes that oxidize misfolded proteins in the cytosol
Nuclear quality control that destroys the mRNA before it is exported
qs.e: Membrane proteins fold in the ER. Misfolded ones are held back, tagged with ubiquitin and sent to the proteasome.

title: Thyroid lab results
passage:
The hypothalamus releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), which stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). TSH stimulates the thyroid gland to make thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃), which raise basal metabolic rate. T₃ and T₄ feed back to inhibit both TRH and TSH secretion.

A clinic measured blood TSH and free T₄ in three patients (Table 1).
cap: Table 1. Lab results compared with normal ranges.

qs.q: Which patient most likely has a problem with the anterior pituitary?
qs.a: Patient 3
w: Patient 1
Patient 2
None of the patients
qs.e: Low TSH should cause low T₄, and low T₄ should normally push TSH up. Both being low points to a pituitary (or hypothalamic) failure to make TSH.

qs.q: Patient 2 has antibodies that bind and activate the TSH receptor. Which symptoms would you expect?
qs.a: Heat intolerance, weight loss and a rapid heart rate
w: Cold intolerance, weight gain and constant fatigue
Low blood calcium, muscle cramps and tingling
High blood sugar, frequent urination and thirst
qs.e: The antibodies drive the thyroid regardless of TSH (as in Graves' disease). High T₄ raises metabolism, and negative feedback suppresses TSH.

qs.q: Long-term dietary iodine deficiency would most likely give lab results like those of:
qs.a: Patient 1
w: Patient 2
Patient 3
No patient, because iodine doesn't affect T₄
qs.e: T₄ needs iodine. Without it, T₄ falls, and the loss of negative feedback raises TSH, which can enlarge the thyroid into a goiter.

qs.q: T₃ acts on target cells mainly by:
qs.a: Binding nuclear receptors that change gene transcription
w: Binding a G protein–coupled receptor on the cell surface
Opening calcium channels in the membrane
Being converted into cAMP
qs.e: Although thyroid hormones are made from amino acids, they are lipophilic and act like steroids, through intracellular receptors.

title: Blue-white screening
passage:
A student inserts a DNA fragment into a plasmid vector. The plasmid carries an ampicillin-resistance gene (ampR) and a copy of lacZ, which encodes β-galactosidase. The cloning site sits inside lacZ, so a successful insert disrupts the gene. β-galactosidase cleaves the colorless compound X-gal into a blue product.

The student mixes the ligation product with E. coli cells that have been made competent and then heat-shocks them. The cells are spread on agar containing ampicillin and X-gal. A control plate gets cells that were heat-shocked without any plasmid.

After overnight growth, the experimental plate has 150 blue colonies and 50 white colonies. The control plate has no colonies.

qs.q: Taking up DNA from the surrounding solution, as the E. coli cells did here, is called:
qs.a: Transformation
w: Conjugation
Transduction
Transposition
qs.e: Transformation is uptake of free DNA. Heat shock and competence treatments make the membrane more permeable to plasmids.

qs.q: Which colonies most likely contain a plasmid with the inserted fragment?
qs.a: The white colonies
w: The blue colonies
Both blue and white colonies equally
Neither, because the insert blocks ampicillin resistance
qs.e: An insert disrupts lacZ, so those cells can't cleave X-gal and stay white. Blue colonies have plasmids with an intact lacZ (no insert).

qs.q: What does the control plate show?
qs.a: That the ampicillin kills cells that lack the plasmid
w: That the X-gal is being cleaved into a blue product
That the DNA fragment was inserted in the right orientation
That heat shock kills E. coli that take up no plasmid
qs.e: No colonies without plasmid means only plasmid-carrying cells survive on ampicillin, so colonies on the experimental plate must contain the plasmid.

qs.q: Ampicillin kills susceptible bacteria by blocking cell-wall synthesis. Why doesn't it harm human cells?
qs.a: Human cells have no peptidoglycan cell wall
w: Human ribosomes are 80S instead of 70S
Human cells pump ampicillin out
Human DNA lacks the ampicillin target sequence
qs.e: β-lactams like ampicillin block cross-linking of peptidoglycan, which only bacteria make. The ribosome difference is the basis for other antibiotics, such as tetracyclines.

title: Blocking the renin–angiotensin system
passage:
When blood pressure or blood flow to the kidney falls, juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (made by the liver) into angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), found mostly on lung capillaries, converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles, stimulates thirst and ADH release, and triggers the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone. Angiotensin II also inhibits renin release.

ACE also breaks down bradykinin, a peptide that dilates blood vessels and can irritate the airways.

In a clinical trial, patients with high blood pressure took an ACE inhibitor daily for 8 weeks.

qs.q: Compared with before treatment, blood renin levels in these patients most likely:
qs.a: Increased, because angiotensin II no longer inhibits renin release
w: Decreased, because ACE inhibitors also block renin release
Stayed the same, because ACE acts after renin in the pathway
Decreased, because lower blood pressure suppresses renin release
qs.e: Less angiotensin II means less negative feedback on juxtaglomerular cells, so renin rises. Lower blood pressure also stimulates renin release.

qs.q: How would the ACE inhibitor most likely affect the kidney's handling of sodium?
qs.a: Less Na⁺ reabsorption, because aldosterone levels fall
w: More Na⁺ reabsorption, because aldosterone levels rise
No change, because ACE acts in the lungs
More Na⁺ reabsorption, because renin rises
qs.e: Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone. Less Na⁺ (and water) is reabsorbed in the distal nephron, which lowers blood volume and pressure.

qs.q: Some patients developed a dry cough. According to the passage, the most likely cause is:
qs.a: Bradykinin building up because ACE no longer breaks it down
w: Angiotensin II building up and constricting the airways
Aldosterone building up and drying out the airway lining
Renin building up and damaging capillaries in the lungs
qs.e: The passage says ACE breaks down bradykinin, which can irritate the airways. Blocking ACE lets bradykinin accumulate.

qs.q: Where does the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II mainly take place?
qs.a: On the capillaries of the lungs
w: In the liver
In the juxtaglomerular cells
In the adrenal cortex
qs.e: The passage says ACE is found mostly on lung capillaries. The liver makes angiotensinogen, and juxtaglomerular cells release renin.

title: Measuring mitochondrial respiration
passage: Researchers isolated mitochondria from rat liver and measured oxygen consumption with an oxygen electrode. Additions were made one after another to the same chamber. Succinate was supplied as the fuel. Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) carries protons across the inner membrane.
cap: Table 1. Oxygen consumption after each sequential addition.

qs.q: Why did adding ADP raise oxygen consumption?
qs.a: ADP lets ATP synthase run, which lets protons back into the matrix so electron transport can speed up
w: ADP donates electrons to Complex I, adding more electrons to the chain so more oxygen is reduced
ADP binds Complex IV directly and raises its affinity for oxygen, so oxygen is reduced faster
ADP makes the inner membrane leaky to protons, so the gradient collapses and respiration speeds up
qs.e: Respiratory control: without ADP, the proton gradient builds up and slows electron transport. Using the gradient to make ATP lets respiration speed up.

qs.q: Why did oligomycin lower oxygen consumption almost to the starting rate?
qs.a: Blocking ATP synthase let the gradient build back up, slowing electron flow
w: Oligomycin binds Complex IV and stops it from passing electrons to oxygen
Oligomycin reacts with succinate and removes the fuel for the electron chain
Oligomycin makes the inner membrane leaky, so protons can't build a gradient
qs.e: Electron transport is coupled to ATP synthesis through the proton gradient. Stopping proton reentry backs up the whole chain.

qs.q: After DNP was added, ATP production would most likely be:
qs.a: Very low, even though oxygen consumption was highest
w: Highest of all the conditions, because O₂ use was highest
The same as with succinate and ADP, since ADP was still present
Higher, because DNP activates ATP synthase as it carries protons
qs.e: DNP lets protons leak back across the membrane without going through ATP synthase (which oligomycin also blocks here). Electron transport races, but the energy is lost as heat.

qs.q: Electrons from succinate enter the chain at Complex II rather than Complex I. Compared with electrons from NADH, they:
qs.a: Pump fewer protons, so they support less ATP synthesis
w: Pump more protons, so they support more ATP synthesis
Pump the same number of protons
Bypass Complex IV
qs.e: Complex II pumps no protons. FADH₂-linked electrons skip Complex I's pumping, so they yield about 1.5 ATP per pair versus about 2.5 for NADH.
